newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan DKB won't comment on racketeer link reports.
newsitem.headline: Japan DKB won't comment on racketeer link reports.

text.p: Major Japanese bank Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank Ltd (DKB) on Monday declined to comment on media reports that it is being questioned by prosecutors over its questionable loans to a racketeer at the centre of the Nomura Securities Co Ltd scandal.
"We do not comment on deals with our individual customers," a bank spokesman said.
Asked if the bank is considering taking legal action over the reports, published in Japanese newspapers at the weekend, the spokesman said there is no such plan.

The daily Mainichi Shimbun reported on Sunday that executives at DKB had been questioned by prosecutors in connection with questionable loans to a principal figure in the Nomura scandal, "sokaiya" Ryuichi Koike.
Koike and his younger brother Yoshinori Koike were arrested last Thursday on suspicion of violating Japan's Commercial Code by taking some 50 million yen in illegal payments from Nomura.
Two former Nomura executives and a third senior Nomura official have also been arrested in the case.
The Commercial Code bans companies from making payments to "sokaiya", racketeers who extort money from companies by threatening to disrupt shareholder meetings.

On Monday, the Mainichi also reported that Ryuichi Koike owned about 20,000 DKB shares under various assumed names, and often attended DKB's annual shareholders' meeting as a "friendly sokaiya". Typically, "friendly sokaiya" uses their influence to stop "enemy sokaiya" from making extortion attempts at annual shareholders' meetings.
The DKB spokesman also declined to confirm whether Ryuichi Koike was a shareholder of the bank.

The Mainichi and other Japanese newspapers have also reported that DKB holds problem loans worth 7.5 billion yen linked to Koike, and also that another financial firm with close ties with DKB has Koike-linked bad loans worth 1.2 billion yen.

Vice Finance Minister Tadashi Ogawa said in a regular news conference on Monday he was aware of the media reports, but said he would not comment as arrests had been made and the matter was under investigation by prosecutors.
"But in general, financial institutions should be careful over their actions as not to invite social criticism as they serve the public," Ogawa said.
After the Nomura payoff scandal was revealed in early March, media reports said DKB loaned three billion yen in 1989 to a real estate company owned by the younger Koike.
The elder Koike reportedly used the money to buy 300,000 shares in each of the nation's top four brokerages including Nomura, and put up the shares as collateral for the DKB loans.

One financial analyst said that if DKB extended loans to the sokaiya without receiving any collateral and was well aware that the loans would not be paid back, it was possible a criminal complaint might be filed.

"If the bank is indicted, the Japanese central government and regional governments may stop business with the bank for a while... In the past, Japanese society was tolerant of banks' wrongdoing, but the times are changing," the analyst said.

The scandal has already cost Nomura, a firm at the heart of Japan's financial system since the 19th century, some of its biggest clients, as corporate and government clients have suspended business with it.
On Monday, DKB shares closed down 50 yen on the Tokyo bourse at 1,470 yen, pressured by newspaper reports over the weekend and on Monday about the bank's questionable loans.
Nomura's shares closed up 20 yen at 1,440.
